Lanes both sides changed are marked with a mergeNote and keep the side whose bytes the gate verifies.
rule: A pinned grammar is its wired bytes (sha256+length), its enumerable surface (id-order, type-set and field-set digests through web-tree-sitter, with the id/named/anonymous vocabularies recorded separately), the local copies those bytes are byte-identical to, the vendored source files (per-file sha256), and the authored provenance/decision record. Verification re-measures all of it and fails on ANY drift — including a vendored source edit, a vanished copy, or a name the vendored source declares that the wired wasm does not have. Regenerating the record is an explicit act (--write), never a silent side effect of verifying.

patches: #743 (rebuildability): `require('tree-sitter-c/grammar')` -> `require('../tree-sitter-c/grammar.js')`. Upstream reads the C grammar through a node_modules entry, and node_modules/ is gitignored repo-wide, so the require made this grammar unrebuildable from a fresh checkout. The C grammar is vendored beside it, so the dependency became a relative path; the same parser.c is generated, with no install step.

#743 (C++ port of the C wave, NARROWED for `::`): a new `macro_prefixed_type_specifier` rule = `prec(-1, seq(alias($.identifier, $.macro_specifier), $._macro_decorated_type))`, with `_macro_decorated_type` restricted to the KEYWORD-LED specifiers (struct/union/enum/class/sized_type_specifier/primitive_type/decltype). The C rule it ports uses the FULL type_specifier, and that breadth does not port: in cpp `_scope_resolution` has an OPTIONAL scope, so `A::B` reads as either the qualified type `A::B` or macro `A` decorating `::B`. Ported verbatim, the new derivation demanded a conflict declaration, and declaring it flipped runtime path selection in unrelated code — `fmt::format_to(std::back_inserter(buf), ...)` parsed as a DECLARATION of a function named `::format_to` in a file with zero ERRORs before and after. `A::B` was never a macro decoration, so the fix removes the ambiguity rather than arbitrating it: restricting the decorated type to keyword-led specifiers makes the bad derivation ungrammatical, and no identifier can start any of them, so no conflict is even possible.

#743 (header name): a `preproc_header_name` token, so a header can be an ARGUMENT of a preprocessor conditional (`#if __has_include(<vector>)`). The rule is scoped to the argument position because `<` cannot BEGIN a preprocessor expression (the unary operators are `! ~ - +`), so no competing `<` token exists there and the header token wins purely on match length; adding `<...>` anywhere in `_preproc_expression` instead would read `< B && C >` as a header name and turn every comparison into something else.
provenance.patchEvidence: The vendored tree is byte-identical to the tree-sitter-cpp@0.23.4 npm tarball for 4 of its 5 files (src/scanner.c cf60387d, tree-sitter.json ce25741b, LICENSE 2e0110e0, package.json bfde98d5) and DIFFERS in exactly one: grammar.js (upstream d0242291 -> vendored 817fc8a0, +54/-2 lines, which is the three patches above and nothing else). The wired wasm is NOT the published bytes: 3,552,974 vs the tarball's 3,434,931, because it was rebuilt with the patches. The fork adds three named node types and no fields — macro_prefixed_type_specifier, macro_specifier, preproc_header_name — with namedIds 256 -> 259, namedUnique 206 -> 209, and an UNCHANGED fieldSetDigest (891be791). The patches are LOAD-BEARING, not cosmetic: over this lane's own 28 cpp fixtures the fork parses 22 clean against upstream's 20, and the two files that separate them are cpp/preproc-has-include.cpp and cpp/macro-decorated-specifier.cpp — the fixtures that were written FOR those two rules, which do not parse at all without them. On the fmt corpus the two agree on all 47 files, so the fork neither helps nor hurts ordinary library C++.

source.note: grammar.js (the FORKED file, see patches) + src/scanner.c + tree-sitter.json + package.json + LICENSE. Four of the five are byte-for-byte from the npm tarball tree-sitter-cpp@0.23.4; grammar.js carries the three #743 patches. The GENERATED src/ (parser.c, grammar.json, node-types.json, tree_sitter/ headers) is NOT vendored, so the offline source<->wasm proof reports `not applicable` for this lane. That is a lane-specific reason, not the generic '41 MB, do not vendor' one the unpatched lanes give: publishing tree-sitter-cpp@0.23.4's own generated JSONs would make the check run and report a PERMANENT three-type delta (macro_prefixed_type_specifier, macro_specifier, preproc_header_name present in the wasm and absent from the source), because the fork's JSONs are what the proof would need and they can only be produced by `tree-sitter generate` from the forked grammar.js. A generated file that must be hand-corrected to make a proof pass is worse than a proof that honestly says it does not apply, so the surface is pinned by the digests below and the fork by the three named types named in the provenance. Rebuild with `tree-sitter generate` then `tree-sitter build --wasm`, from a tree that also has grammars/tree-sitter-c present — grammar.js requires ../tree-sitter-c/grammar.js, so unlike every unpatched lane this one is NOT rebuildable from its own directory alone.

cpp.decision: Pin as-is, as a local rebuild from vendored source with the patch set recorded. The wired bytes are not the published release and must not be recorded as such: a reader who ran `npm pack tree-sitter-cpp@0.23.4` and compared would find a 118 KB difference and no way to account for it, which is precisely the failure M63.5 (#954, 'bind corpus measurements to a grammar hash') is about. The patch set is small, fully enumerated above, and provably load-bearing, so the honest record is the base version PLUS the patches — not the base version alone, which is what the analyzer's own documentation claimed until this entry existed ('Parser: tree-sitter-cpp 0.23.4 (npm, latest)'). A version-only string cannot express a fork, and tree-sitter.json's own `metadata.version: 0.23.4` does not either.

patches: FIX 1 (§3.18) `extend schema` gains `repeat1(root_operation_type_definition)` and an optional body, with `prec.right` for the `{` ambiguity — fixes `extend schema { query: Q mutation: M }` and Apollo Federation's bodyless `extend schema @link(...)`

FIX 3 (§3.3) `field`'s `optional($.directive)` becomes `optional($.directives)` — `{ f @a @b }` is the legal spelling of two directives on one selection
FIX 4 (§2.9.4) both string rules learn their escapes: the short string accepts `\` + any non-newline, the block string accepts `"""` and skips `\` as a unit

provenance.patchEvidence: Each FIX is one row of a 113-construct battery that names the specification section and states whether the construct is valid, so a failure can be classified as a GRAMMAR GAP (valid, rejected) or a CORRECT REJECTION (invalid, correctly rejected) rather than lumped together. Before/after on that battery: the previous wasm rejected 10 valid constructs, upstream `main` rejects 6, this build rejects 0, and all three reject the same 8 invalid constructs. The four FIXes were each confirmed to be necessary by building upstream and watching that construct fail there too. Artifacts: fixtures/graphql/out/grammar-gaps.json, fixtures/graphql/out/grammar-ab.json, fixtures/graphql/out/extraction-ab.json.

source.note: grammar.upstream.js (bkegley/tree-sitter-graphql@ee5ce96, VERBATIM — the fixed input, so the port is idempotent) + port.py (the patch AS CODE: the rename table and the four anchored FIX hunks, each refusing to write a half-ported grammar) + grammar.js (the GENERATED patched grammar, which is what `tree-sitter generate` reads) + tree-sitter.json (ABI 15) + package.json (deliberately no `"type"` field: the repo root is `"type": "module"` and grammar.js is CommonJS `module.exports`, so without a local package.json the tree-sitter CLI cannot load it) + LICENSE (MIT) + README.md (the divergence record, the regeneration sequence, and what the patch bought) + src/grammar.json + src/node-types.json. The two generated JSONs are vendored ON PURPOSE: `sourceVsWasmFor` needs the pair to run the offline source<->wasm proof, and without them the check reports `not applicable` and this lane has no such proof at all. src/parser.c IS vendored (284 KB), the same call hcl made at 600 KB and the opposite of nim at 41 MB: `measureVendored` hashes every file in the tree, tracked or not, so an untracked parser.c would turn the gate red after any `tree-sitter generate`. Tracking it makes the wired wasm rebuildable from TRACKED files alone and keeps the recorded digests still across a regeneration that changed nothing else. The exact three-command sequence is in README.md. A `node_modules` symlink points at the tree-sitter CLI during a build and is not tracked.

graphql.decision: Pin the local rebuild of the PATCHED vendored source. (1) The offline source<->wasm proof runs and is zero in both directions on the declared named types, re-measured by this gate on every run: every name the committed source declares exists in the wired wasm, and every wasm-named type is declared by the source. That is the offline statement that the committed bytes ARE a build of the committed source. (2) The wired build rejects 0 of 113 specification constructs, against 10 for the wasm it replaces and 6 for upstream `main`, while still correctly rejecting all 8 invalid constructs — so the patch is a strict improvement on BOTH the previous build and upstream, and does not trade correctness for permissiveness. (3) The extraction A/B over 47 real files, same analyzer both sides, moves 12 error files to 4, 20 error nodes to 7, and ADDS 4 symbols and 76 relationships; every single delta is enumerated and adjudicated in fixtures/graphql/REVIEW.md §E, and the direction is uniform. (4) The two most consequential upstream gaps (`interface I implements J`; a description on a `schema` block) both produced PUBLISHED PHANTOMS in the previous build, not merely missing facts, so this is a correctness pin and not a completeness one. (5) The PascalCase surface is preserved exactly, so no analyzer string literal, no stored symbol row and no m12/m14/m60 lane changes spelling — the one thing an upgrade must not do to this repository.

alternatives.option: pin the previous wasm as-is and document the two gaps as boundaries (what docs/analyzers/real-graphql-analyzer.md did)
alternatives.measured: REJECTED on evidence: 12 of 47 corpus files carry a grammar error under it, and the losses are not silent — on neo4j-graphql/.../apollo-federation-subgraph-compatibility/schema.graphql a described `extend type User` became ERROR and the analyzer published `anonymous_operation_1566 -> Int`, `-> ID`, `-> @external`, `-> @requires` (four invented references) while losing five real field symbols. A documented boundary is the right answer for a gap nobody can fix; a 12/47 error rate with phantom edges is not that.

alternatives.option: upgrade to bkegley/tree-sitter-graphql main (ee5ce96) unmodified
alternatives.measured: REJECTED on capability, and this is the load-bearing measurement of the lane: upstream names its rules snake_case (`object_type_definition`). The analyzer, the m12 shape-safety census, the m14 and m60 lanes and every stored symbol row assume `ObjectTypeDefinition`. Building upstream unmodified and running the node-type set difference gives 72 node types gained and 72 lost with identical names apart from casing — i.e. every construct routes through the analyzer's default arm and the file yields nothing. It also leaves 6 of its own gaps (ext-schema-multi, ext-schema-directives-only, ext-scalar, desc-block-escaped-triple, field-two-directives, apollo-link).

alternatives.option: hand-edit the vendored grammar.js in place, the way groovy's was hand-repaired
alternatives.measured: REJECTED on reviewability, and the difference is not cosmetic. A hand edit leaves no record of what upstream did, is not re-derivable when upstream moves, and cannot be diffed as a patch. port.py keeps the upstream file verbatim, expresses the patch as four anchored hunks plus a rename table, refuses to write a half-ported grammar when an anchor is missing, and re-derives grammar.js byte-identically on every run. Same bytes, reviewable provenance.

alternatives.measured: It is not, and that is the finding rather than a workaround: the previous wasm predates `optional($.description)` on `schema_definition` and `optional($.directives)` on `variable_definition`, so it was built from a commit bkegley no longer has a tag for and which the GitHub API does not surface. The previous wasm is kept byte-for-byte at fixtures/graphql/grammar-rebuild/tree-sitter-graphql-VENDORED-BEFORE.wasm (sha256 9cd70f691576f0217834e62cd584bac603971d4c1889cbf068a1029ff2855b27) so the A/B against it is reproducible forever.

nim.decision: Pin the local rebuild, and the reason is a PROOF rather than a preference. (1) The vendored src/node-types.json declares exactly the named types the wired wasm materialises, and the wired wasm declares exactly the named types that source declares - zero in both directions, re-measured by this gate on every run. That is the offline statement that the committed bytes ARE a build of the committed source. (2) The wired build parses all 17 compiler-validated construct-matrix files with 0 ERROR and 0 MISSING, and every file in that matrix was first ACCEPTED by the real Nim 2.2.12 compiler (`nim check`), so a construct the compiler rejects could never be counted as evidence. (3) The grammar's own conformance suite passes 72/72 here. (4) The three other published tree-sitter-nim grammars were all cloned, generated and built, and each is rejected on a MEASURED ground: aMOPel cannot be loaded at all by the pinned runtime, haxscramper emits ZERO fields and 283 ERROR / 7 MISSING over the matrix because it transcribes the ABNF tokens of doc/grammar.txt as node types, and reo101 is a 9-line stub. (5) The external scanner makes a shared-parser lifecycle a live question rather than an assumption, so it was MEASURED: a fresh-parser-per-file reference against one shared parser over 47 files in two orders (file order, and a rotated order putting a different layout shape before each file) produced 0 differences in both, so the engine's cached-parser path is safe for nim and needs no lua-style isolation. Full table, the per-candidate numbers and the reproduction commands: grammars/tree-sitter-nim/PIN.md.

vb.decision: Pin as a local rebuild of a patched vendored source, and say plainly that this is the weakest pin in the file. There is no upstream release to pin: the repository publishes no npm package and no tagged release, and it is a 2-star project whose last push predates this lane. The wired bytes are therefore NOT byte-identical to anything published -- they are a build of a source this repo owns, and the pin's value is drift detection over THAT source (a hand edit to grammar.js moves the recorded digest and fails the gate) plus the source<->wasm proof that the committed bytes really are a build of the committed grammar. What the pin deliberately does NOT claim: that this is the best available VB.NET grammar. It is the best of the two that exist and the only one measured to parse real VB.NET at all (the alternative measured 29.50 % clean on the same draw), and it is NOT finished -- 90.89 % aggregate clean over 1185 files with 0 crash files, so roughly one file in eleven still carries an ERROR. The gate's floor is the number that has to move, and the long-tail defect census (fixtures/probes/defect-census.ts) is the work list that has to shrink it.

alternatives.option: leave `.vb` routed to `__generic__` and ship no grammar
alternatives.measured: rejected, and this is the status quo that motivated the lane: a regex generic analyzer over VB.NET. A generic pass cannot see a Class, a Function, an Implements clause or a call site, so the lane publishes no symbols and no relationships for .vb files at all -- and it does so QUIETLY, because the file is detected and 'analysed' rather than refused. That is the failure the M60 routing ruling names: an extension routed to a parser that cannot represent its format is reported as covered.

alternatives.measured: rejected on measurement, not on stars. Its grammar also had no `supertypes` and no `word` token, both of which the analyzer will want.

patches: REPAIR 1 (scanner, `common/scanner.h` `scan_pi_content`): the trailing `advance_if_eq(lexer, '\n')` became `skip_if_eq`. `advance_if_eq` is defined as `if (!eof && lookahead==chr) advance(lexer); else return false`, so its `else` ABORTS the caller — and the caller had already committed, past `mark_end`, on a lookahead whose value is irrelevant. A processing instruction with content therefore produced no `_pi_content` token, `<?target content?>` could not complete, and the parser wrapped the whole `<?...?>` in an ERROR node. It was not merely a lost declaration: with no XMLDecl present the enclosing `prolog` node disappeared too, taking any DOCTYPE in the same prolog with it. A 19-shape battery isolates it exactly: the construct parses iff the byte after `?>` is `\n` (fixtures/xml/out/pi-rootcause.json). `check_word` and `scan_comment` keep `advance_if_eq`, where a mismatch correctly means "not the token I was asked for".

REPAIR 2 (grammar, `xml/grammar.js` `_intSubset`): the internal subset is now `repeat(choice($._markupdecl, $.conditionalSect, $._DeclSep))` over a named `_intSubsetItem` rule, and `conditionalSect` is declared. Upstream could not reach a conditional section from an internal subset at ANY version measured: 0.5.0-0.6.x declare `conditionalSect` in the `dtd` grammar and inline it, but `_intSubset` referenced `$._markupdecl`, which does not include it; 0.7.0, which the wired wasm matches exactly, does not declare it in the `xml` grammar at all. The failure was destructive, not silent: `<![INCLUDE[...]]>` wrapped the `doctypedecl` in an ERROR and the parser then took a LATER `Name` as the DTD's name, so the analyzer published a Type symbol literally named `INCLUDE`. The named `_intSubsetItem` is because tree-sitter rejects a rule that can match the empty string and XML 1.0 permits an empty internal subset; writing the repeat at each use site keeps the generated `node-types.json` free of a wrapper node.
provenance.patchEvidence: Two A/Bs, both over the whole pinned corpus, both re-runnable. (1) CONSTRUCT A/B: 29 shapes across the wired wasm, a build of upstream v0.5.0, a build of upstream HEAD v0.7.0, and this build — the wired wasm and upstream HEAD are byte-IDENTICAL in behaviour on all of them, which is what pins the pre-repair bytes as an unmodified upstream build (fixtures/xml/out/grammar-ab.json). (2) CORPUS A/B: 8,888 files / 33.6 MB / 6.69 M nodes across 6 repos, counting ERROR and MISSING per file: 31 files repaired, 2 files moved the wrong way, 8,855 unchanged, and corpus MISSING nodes 32 -> 10 (fixtures/xml/out/grammar-corpus-ab.json). xml.decision: Pin the local rebuild of the PATCHED vendored source, and record that the pre-repair bytes needed no provenance work at all. (1) The pre-repair wired wasm is an UNMODIFIED upstream build: its enumerable surface is byte-for-byte the surface of a build of upstream HEAD 0.7.0 (140 node types, 2 fields, zero set difference in either direction) and its behaviour matches that build on all 29 constructs of the A/B battery. So unlike Groovy this was not a stale blob; it was current upstream, and the two defects are UPSTREAM defects that upstream's own test corpus never exercises — `grep -rn 'PITarget' test/corpus/` returns nothing, and the only `PI`-adjacent tests are `StyleSheetPI`/`XmlModelPI`. (2) Because the defects are upstream's, no upgrade fixes them: v0.5.0, v0.6.4 and v0.7.0 all fail both, which is the measurement that makes the repair necessary rather than optional. (3) Upgrading past 0.7.0 would DELETE capability, not add it: 0.7.0 already split DTD into a separate `dtd` grammar, and adopting a split would strand `elementdecl`, `AttlistDecl`, `AttDef`, `GEDecl`, `PEDecl` and `NotationDecl` — the analyzer's entire DTD surface — in a grammar this engine does not wire. (4) The repair is admissible on the corpus A/B above: 31 files repaired against 2 adjudicated out-of-surface/negative-control movements, and corpus MISSING nodes down 32 -> 10. (5) The offline source<->wasm proof runs and is measured on every gate run.

alternatives.option: pin the pre-repair bytes as-is and document the two defects as boundaries (what docs/analyzers/real-xml-analyzer.md does today)
alternatives.measured: REJECTED on capability, and the cost is the whole declaration vocabulary of a DTD. A content-bearing processing instruction is one of the most common constructs in XML, and it does not merely lose a symbol: with no XMLDecl present the enclosing `prolog` node is destroyed, so `<!DOCTYPE …>` in the same prolog is lost with it, and in a conditional section the parser picks a later `Name` as the DTD name and the analyzer publishes a Type symbol called `INCLUDE`. A documented boundary is right for a gap nobody can fix; this one is fixable in two lines and the fix is measured.

alternatives.option: upgrade to upstream HEAD 0.7.0 unmodified
alternatives.measured: REJECTED, and this is the negative result worth keeping: the pre-repair wired bytes ALREADY ARE 0.7.0. Surface-identical (140 types, 2 fields, zero difference either way) and behaviourally identical on all 29 battery constructs, so the upgrade buys nothing — and it leaves both defects in place, because they are upstream's. Separately, 0.7.0's split of DTD into its own `dtd` grammar means the `xml` grammar alone cannot represent a standalone `.dtd` file at all (root node type ERROR, measured), which is filed as a separate finding rather than solved by a swap.

alternatives.option: hand-edit the vendored grammar in place, the way groovy's was hand-repaired
alternatives.measured: REJECTED on re-derivability, and it matters more here than for Groovy. Both repairs are in files a future `tree-sitter generate` or upstream sync would otherwise be diffed against, and REPAIR 2 changes a GRAMMAR RULE (so `src/parser.c` is regenerated) while REPAIR 1 changes a SCANNER HEADER (so it is not). A hand edit leaves no record of which is which; the patch list above, the PIN.md record and the per-file digests below make the divergence from 0.7.0 auditable in one read, and `common/scanner.h` is 155 lines of upstream source so the delta is three added lines and one changed line.

alternatives.option: wire upstream's separate `dtd` grammar as a second language for `.dtd`
alternatives.measured: NOT TAKEN, and recorded as owed rather than rejected. It is measurably the right grammar — it parses libxml2's `cond_sect1.dtd` and `cond_sect2.dtd`, which the `xml` grammar cannot represent at all (root ERROR, 11 and 8 ERROR nodes), with 0 ERROR nodes — but it is a new wired language, a new router entry, a new analyzer and a new lane, not a repair. The measurement is kept so the decision is revisit-able with numbers instead of a recollection.

patches: P1 (grammar/statements/): `CONSTRAINT <name> UNIQUE | FOREIGN KEY | INDEX`. The only rule accepting a leading `CONSTRAINT <name>` accepted just `PRIMARY KEY` and `CHECK`, so the two most common named constraints in a real schema lost their names.
P2 (grammar/statements/): `DELETE FROM t AS x` and `DELETE FROM t USING o`.
P3 (grammar/statements/): `grant_statement` / `revoke_statement` as VISIBLE nodes (upstream had the rules hidden, so the analyzer's GRANT/REVOKE arms named node types that no file could produce).

P4 (grammar/statements/do-drop-policy.js): `do_statement` and `drop_policy`. `keyword_do` existed but was wired only to MySQL's `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY DO UPDATE`; `keyword_policy` existed (create_policy needs it) but no drop rule used it.

patches: P1 (#743, grammar.js): `macro_prefixed_type_specifier` as a VISIBLE node, with the conflict entries the ordinary reading (`A B;` = a B of type A) needs. Upstream hides the rule, so the analyzer could not name the type position at all; the `#743` note in the vendored file records that two conflict variants became unnecessary once the rule carried `prec(-1)`.

P2 (#743b, grammar.js): a header name in a PREPROCESSOR-ARGUMENT position -- `__has_include(<vector>)`, `__has_include("meta")` and the wrapper form `FMT_HAS_INCLUDE(<string_view>)`. Upstream parses every one of these as an ERROR node, because `<string_view>` is not a preproc expression: `<` would have to be a binary operator with a missing left operand. The shape reaches 16 files across the two cpp corpora, in the guard of every portable header. Scoped to the ARGUMENT position deliberately: `<` cannot BEGIN a `_preproc_expression` (the unary operators are `! ~ - +`), so there is no competing `<` token to lose the tie to at the start of an argument.
provenance.patchEvidence: Surface and behaviour A/B over three builds, re-runnable via `bun run script/m14/tmp/c-audit/c-grammar-pin.ts` (artifact: validation/m14/results/c-grammar-pin.json). WIRED vs a REBUILD of this committed patched source: named-type surface IDENTICAL in both directions (128 named types, zero difference either way) -- the byte sha256s differ, as they must, because a wasm build carries its emscripten version, compiler flags and section order; identity is claimed on surface and behaviour, which is what this gate measures. WIRED vs pristine tree-sitter-c@0.24.1's own published wasm: 3 named types present in WIRED and absent from pristine -- `macro_prefixed_type_specifier`, `macro_specifier`, `preproc_header_name` -- and ZERO the other way, which is the statement that the patch is live in the bytes this lane loads and is purely additive at the node-type level. 10-construct behavioural battery, WIRED == REBUILD on all 10, and the 3 `#743b` shapes are `damaged` under pristine and `clean` under both WIRED and REBUILD, while the two comparison shapes the patch could have broken (`#if A < B && C > D`, `#if MAX(A < B, C < D)`) and all 5 controls are `clean` under all three. The pristine and rebuilt wasms are kept at fixtures/c/grammar/ with a SHA256SUMS.txt so the A/B survives any network copy disappearing.

source.note: grammar.js -- the PATCHED upstream 0.24.1 grammar, carrying this repository's own #743/#743b edits and their measured rationale in comments, not a pristine copy -- plus src/grammar.json and src/node-types.json REGENERATED from that patched grammar.js by `tree-sitter generate` (tree-sitter CLI 0.25.10) on 2026-09-29, plus package.json, tree-sitter.json and LICENSE byte-identical to npm tree-sitter-c@0.24.1. The generated src/ is the point of the exercise: before it, the vendored tree carried no node-types.json/grammar.json pair, so this gate's source<->wasm check could not run for C at all and the lane had no offline proof that its bytes were a build of its own source. src/parser.c (3.9 MB) is deliberately NOT vendored -- `tree-sitter generate` rebuilds it from grammar.js, and the check runs on the generated JSONs.

c.decision: Pin as a LOCAL REBUILD OF THE PATCHED VENDORED SOURCE, and the reason is that the prior question had to be answered before provenance could be stated at all. `wasm/tree-sitter-c.wasm` (650,175 B, sha256 f9a2d771...) was recorded in validation/m14/results/wasm-provenance-census.json with NO byte-identical local copy and the verdict "provenance cannot be re-derived offline", while grammars/tree-sitter-c/ carried only grammar.js/LICENSE/package.json/tree-sitter.json, so this gate could not compare the source to the bytes either. `byte-identical-to-npm-tarball` -- the kind every other lane in this file uses -- was therefore unavailable: the vendored grammar.js differs from npm tree-sitter-c@0.24.1's by 75 diff lines and carries this repository's #743/#743b markers. So the real question was whether the WIRED bytes are a build of the PATCHED source or a pristine build predating the patch, and it decides what every C measurement means, because the F1 oracle, the 2,498-file census, the clang layout probe and all 28 mutants are all measurements of a parse produced by these bytes. Measured answer: the patch IS live. A rebuild of the committed patched source is surface-identical to WIRED in both directions (128 named types) and behaviourally identical on all 10 constructs, while pristine upstream differs by exactly the 3 node types the patch adds and fails all 3 `#743b` shapes. The consequence is the useful one: the incumbent was already a verified build, so no C measurement needs re-baselining, and had the wired bytes matched pristine the #743b fix would not have been live and the whole lane would have needed re-measuring. This also retires a live hazard recorded in this wave's own review: the #936 defect was a node-type literal (`attributed_type_specifier`) written from memory of a different tree-sitter-c release, which F1 caught only because the vocabulary happened to be checked -- the pin makes the release explicit rather than remembered.

alternatives.option: Adopt npm tree-sitter-c@0.24.1's own published wasm (sha c852c2a8..., 625,918 B) as the wired bytes
alternatives.measured: REJECTED, and this is the load-bearing measurement of the lane: it DELETES capability. It is 3 named types short of the wired bytes -- `macro_prefixed_type_specifier`, `macro_specifier`, `preproc_header_name` -- and it parses all three `#743b` shapes as ERROR nodes where the wired build parses them clean. The first is a node the C analyzer itself names (the `macro_prefixed_type_specifier` note in the vendored grammar.js is a #743 record, and the analyzer's member/enumerator rules key on macro names), and the second is 16 files across the two cpp corpora whose portable-header guards would move from clean to damaged.

alternatives.option: Pin the wired bytes as `unnamed-build-sha-only`
alternatives.measured: REJECTED as insufficient, not as wrong. It would record the sha256 and stop, which does protect against future drift -- but it leaves the central question open, and the answer turned out to be available and cheap: the patch is live, the source is in-tree, and a rebuild reproduces the bytes' surface and behaviour exactly. A sha-only pin on bytes that are demonstrably a build of committed source understates what is actually known.

alternatives.option: Regenerate the wired bytes from the patched source and adopt the rebuild
alternatives.measured: NOT NEEDED, and worth recording as a negative result. The rebuild is 630,720 B against the wired 650,175 B -- a toolchain difference, not a grammar difference -- with identical surface and identical behaviour on all 10 constructs. Swapping would have churned every C measurement for no observable gain, and the pin does not require byte identity: it requires that the committed source and the committed bytes agree, which the gate now re-measures on every run.
